ABSTRACT

The rapid depletion of natural mineral aggregates alongside the annual generation of over 3.0 billion tonnes of Construction and Demolition (C&D) waste presents a severe sustainability challenge. Utilizing Recycled Aggregates (RA) derived from crushed concrete, brick, and mortar provides a sustainable alternative, but their structural use in pavement subgrades and concrete is hindered by unpredictable particle crushing under mechanical compaction.

Conventional single-particle crushing tests using a laboratory Universal Testing Machine (UTM) and mechanical sieve shakers are destructive, labor-intensive (taking 16–24 hours per batch), hazardous due to respirable silica dust, and unable to evaluate continuous variations in particle geometry.

This project develops an end-to-end Physics-Informed Machine Learning (PIML) suite to predict single-particle crushing mechanics and post-breakage particle size distributions without laboratory destruction. By mathematically coupling size-dependent Weibull brittle fracture statistics (Liang et al., 2025) with 3D shape-dependent power laws (Cai et al., 2024) across three waste materials—Recycled Concrete (RC), Recycled Brick (RB), and Recycled Mortar (RM)—a benchmark dataset of $N = 3,600$ particles ($4.75\text{–}37.5\text{ mm}$) was established.

Six regression models (Ridge Polynomial, Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost, and Physics-Informed MLP) were trained to predict Crushing Strength ($\sigma_f$), Peak Rupture Force ($F_f$), Crushing Energy ($E_f$), and Post-Breakage Fractal Gradation Dimension ($D$). CatBoost achieved the highest overall performance (Mean $R^2 = 0.962$, $\sigma_f$ MAPE = $5.81\%$, $F_f$ $R^2 = 0.987$). Game-theoretic SHAP and partial dependence analyses confirm that models respect physical fracture laws: sphericity ($\Phi$) dictates crushing strength, while contact diameter ($d_0$) governs peak force through Hiramatsu-Oka quadratic scaling ($F_f \propto d_0^2$). Against real published laboratory benchmarks, the continuous model achieves an MAE of $0.043\text{ MPa}$ and MAPE of $1.15\%$.

The trained engine was integrated into an interactive web application featuring a Virtual UTM & Sieve Lab, a Multi-Scale Scaling Simulator, an auxiliary Computer Vision Scanner, and a model benchmark dashboard, reducing testing duration by $>100,000\times$ and eliminating material destruction.

Keywords: Recycled Aggregates, Physics-Informed Machine Learning, Single-Particle Crushing, Weibull Size Effect, Fractal Gradation, Hiramatsu-Oka Equation, Virtual Testing Laboratory.

1. INTRODUCTION

1.1 Background and Problem Statement

The global construction industry consumes over 50 billion tonnes of natural aggregates annually, causing severe depletion of riverbed sand and quarry deposits, riverbank erosion, and groundwater degradation. Concurrently, urban renewal generates over 3.0 billion tonnes of Construction and Demolition (C&D) waste each year. Recycling demolition rubble into Recycled Aggregates (RA) offers an indispensable circular solution.

However, recycled aggregate consists of three heterogeneous materials: 1. Recycled Concrete (RC): Natural stone partially coated with adhered, porous cement mortar. 2. Recycled Brick (RB): Porous, brittle fired clay masonry fragments. 3. Recycled Mortar (RM): Friable sand-cement conglomerate with high porosity and low strength.

Because of pre-existing micro-cracks from demolition, recycled aggregates exhibit high water absorption ($5\% - 15\%$) and erratic single-particle crushing strength. Standard civil engineering codes severely restrict their use in pavement subgrades, railway ballast, and structural concrete due to concerns over unpredictable mechanical degradation under compaction.

1.2 Limitations of Conventional Physical Testing

To evaluate aggregate degradation, standard practice involves single-particle diametral compression tests using a Universal Testing Machine (UTM) followed by mechanical sieve analysis: - Destructive: Testing permanently destroys specimens, preventing repeated testing under varied conditions. - Extreme Statistical Scatter: Flaws cause crushing strengths of identical-sized stones to vary by $300\% - 500\%$. - Time and Labor Intensive: Sizing, testing, and sieving 100 particles requires 16 to 24 hours of manual labor. - Health Hazard: Dry crushing and sieving produce hazardous airborne respirable crystalline silica dust. - Discrete Bins: Laboratory sieves only test discrete size brackets, failing to capture continuous 3D shape variations.

1.3 Proposed Solution: Physics-Informed Virtual Testing

To address these limitations, this project develops a Physics-Informed Machine Learning (PIML) platform. Purely data-driven machine learning models frequently produce non-physical outputs when extrapolating. By embedding established geomechanical laws—specifically the Hiramatsu-Oka stress conversion, Weibull weakest-link scaling, Bagheri equivalent diameter, Cai shape power laws, and Tyler-Wheatcraft fractal fragmentation—the learning models are constrained to respect fundamental fracture mechanics.

1.4 Project Objectives

  1. Coupled Dataset Generation: Synthesize a benchmark dataset ($N = 3,600$) coupling size-dependent Weibull fracture (Liang et al., 2025) and 3D shape-dependent crushing strength and energy (Cai et al., 2024).
  2. Machine Learning Benchmarking: Train and validate six regression models and three classifiers to predict Crushing Strength ($\sigma_f$), Failure Force ($F_f$), Crushing Energy ($E_f$), and Fractal Dimension ($D$).
  3. Mechanistic Verification: Use game-theoretic SHAP and partial dependence analyses to confirm that models honor physical laws.
  4. Interactive Virtual Testing Software: Deploy an open-source Streamlit web application providing a Virtual UTM, an Inverse Design Scaling Simulator, an auxiliary Computer Vision scanner, and an automated validation suite.

2. THEORETICAL FORMULATIONS & GOVERNING MECHANICS

2.1 Single-Particle Diametral Loading & Hiramatsu-Oka Equation

When an irregular aggregate particle is compressed between flat, rigid steel platens in a testing machine, localized compressive stresses at contact points induce internal tensile stresses normal to the loading axis. Hiramatsu and Oka (1966) derived the classical relationship relating peak compressive failure force $F_f$ to internal tensile crushing strength $\sigma_f$: $$\sigma_f = 0.9 \frac{F_f}{d_0^2} \quad \implies \quad F_f = \frac{\sigma_f \cdot d_0^2}{0.9}$$ where $\sigma_f$ is crushing strength in MPa, $F_f$ is peak force in N, and $d_0$ is the effective platen gauge diameter in mm.

2.2 Bagheri Contact Gauge Diameter

For irregular particles with tri-axial dimensions $L \ge I \ge S > 0$, the volumetric equivalent spherical diameter is $d_{eq} = \sqrt[3]{L \cdot I \cdot S}$. Bagheri et al. (2015) established an empirical roughness correction mapping $d_{eq}$ to the true platen contact gauge diameter $d_0$: $$d_0 = 0.887 \sqrt[3]{L \cdot I \cdot S} = 0.887 \cdot d_{eq}$$ This formulation was verified and adopted by Liang et al. (2025) for recycled demolition waste particles.

2.3 3D Particle Morphology & Zingg Classification

From the orthogonal dimensions ($L, I, S$), standard shape descriptors are defined: - Elongation Index: $EI = I / L$ - Flatness Index: $FI = S / I$ - True Sphericity: $\Phi = \sqrt[3]{\frac{I \cdot S}{L^2}}$ (where $\Phi = 1.0$ for a perfect sphere)

Zingg (1935) classified particle shapes into four geometric quadrants using the $0.67$ boundary: 1. Disk (Oblate): $EI < 0.67, FI \ge 0.67$ 2. Block (Equant): $EI \ge 0.67, FI \ge 0.67$ 3. Blade (Tri-axial): $EI < 0.67, FI < 0.67$ 4. Bar (Prolate): $EI \ge 0.67, FI < 0.67$

2.4 Weibull Statistical Size Scaling

In brittle materials, failure initiates at pre-existing Griffith micro-flaws. Larger aggregate particles possess a higher statistical probability of containing a catastrophic flaw, leading to reduced nominal strength. The survival probability $P_s(\sigma)$ is modeled via Weibull's distribution: $$P_s(\sigma) = \exp \left[ - \left( \frac{\sigma}{\sigma_{f0}} \right)^m \right]$$ where $\sigma_{f0}$ is characteristic strength ($36.8\%$ survival stress) and $m$ is the Weibull modulus. Liang et al. (2025) measured characteristic strengths across sieve brackets (Table 2.1).

Table 2.1: Experimental Weibull Parameters (Liang et al., 2025 Table 2)

Sieve Bracket (mm) RC: $\sigma_{f0}$ (MPa), $m$ RB: $\sigma_{f0}$ (MPa), $m$ RM: $\sigma_{f0}$ (MPa), $m$
4.75 – 10.0 6.51 MPa, $m = 1.58$ 6.35 MPa, $m = 2.58$ 3.03 MPa, $m = 2.70$
10.0 – 20.0 6.28 MPa, $m = 1.30$ 6.21 MPa, $m = 2.61$ 2.97 MPa, $m = 2.73$
20.0 – 25.0 6.07 MPa, $m = 1.25$ 4.92 MPa, $m = 3.32$ 2.91 MPa, $m = 2.76$

2.5 Cai et al. (2024) Shape-Strength Power Law

Cai et al. (2024) demonstrated that crushing strength scales with sphericity $\Phi$ via a power law at reference size ($d_{ref} \approx 25\text{ mm}$): $$\sigma_f(\Phi) = p \cdot \Phi^q$$ Calibrated values: RC: $p = 9.35, q = 2.13$ ($R^2 = 0.99$); RM: $p = 4.69, q = 2.21$ ($R^2 = 0.98$); RB: $p = 3.84, q = 1.68$ ($R^2 = 0.90$).

Coupling shape-strength with Weibull size-scaling yields our unified crushing strength equation: $$\sigma_f(d_0, \Phi) = \left[ p \cdot \Phi^q \right] \times \left[ \frac{\sigma_{f0}(d_0)}{\sigma_{f0,\text{ref}}} \right]$$

2.6 Tyler-Wheatcraft Fractal Fragmentation Gradation

Upon crushing, fragments follow scale-invariant fractal distributions (Tyler & Wheatcraft, 1992). The cumulative mass percentage $F(d)$ passing a sieve opening $d$ is: $$F(d) = \left( \frac{d}{d_0} \right)^{3 - D} \times 100\%$$ where $D$ is the post-breakage fractal dimension ($1.5 \le D \le 2.7$). Lower $D$ ($\approx 1.8$) indicates clean cleavage into a few large pieces; higher $D$ ($\approx 2.5$) indicates severe shattering into fine dust.

3. DATASET GENERATION & MACHINE LEARNING PIPELINE

3.1 Physics-Coupled Dataset Generation ($N = 3,600$)

Using the governing equations, a balanced benchmark dataset of $N = 3,600$ single particles was synthesized: - 1,200 particles each for Recycled Concrete (RC), Recycled Brick (RB), and Recycled Mortar (RM). - Spanning three nominal sieve fractions: $4.75\text{–}9.5\text{ mm}$, $9.5\text{–}19.0\text{ mm}$, and $19.0\text{–}37.5\text{ mm}$. - Dimensions ($L, I, S$) generated from truncated normal distributions based on Cai et al. empirical means with $CV_L = 12\%, CV_I = 10\%, CV_S = 13\%$, sorted descending to enforce $L \ge I \ge S > 0$. - Targets generated per sample: Crushing Strength ($\sigma_f$), Peak Force ($F_f$), Crushing Energy ($E_f$), Fractal Dimension ($D$), Breakage Mode (Mode I Splitting, Mode II Corner Rupture, Mode III Fragmentation), and cumulative passing for 12 standard sieves ($0.075\text{ mm}$ to $37.5\text{ mm}$).

3.2 Feature Vector & Pre-Processing

Each particle is described by a 16-dimensional feature vector: - Continuous Features (13): $L, I, S, EI, FI, \Phi, S_f, d_{eq}, d_0, \rho_a, \rho_b, E, \nu$. - Categorical Features (3): Material_Enc (RC/RB/RM), Shape_Class_Enc (Disk/Block/Blade/Bar), Sieve_Bracket_Enc.

Data was split into an $80\%$ training set ($N_{train} = 2,880$) and a $20\%$ unseen test set ($N_{test} = 720$) using stratified sampling based on breakage mode. Continuous features were scaled using z-score normalization fitted strictly on the training partition.

3.3 Model Architectures & Benchmarking Results

Six regression architectures were tuned and evaluated using 5-fold cross-validation: 1. Ridge Polynomial Regression (Baseline): Degree-2 polynomial expansion ($16 \to 152$ features), $\alpha = 1.0$. 2. Random Forest: 200 trees, max_depth = 15, min_samples_split = 5. 3. XGBoost: 300 boosted trees, learning rate $\eta = 0.05$, max_depth = 8, $\alpha = 0.1, \lambda = 1.0$. 4. LightGBM: 300 boosting rounds, learning rate $\eta = 0.05$, max_depth = 8. 5. CatBoost (Best Overall): 300 iterations, learning rate $\eta = 0.05$, depth = 8, L2 leaf reg = 3.0. 6. Physics-Informed MLP: Architecture 16 → 128 → 64 → 32 → 1, ReLU, Adam optimizer, early stopping.

3.4 Model Explainability via SHAP Analysis

To confirm models learned physical mechanics rather than statistical artifacts, SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) feature attributions were calculated (Figure 3.2): - Crushing Strength ($\sigma_f$): Sphericity ($\Phi$) dominates with $>45\%$ feature attribution, confirming that contact stress concentration at sharp corners dictates ultimate strength. - Peak Force ($F_f$): Bagheri contact diameter ($d_0$) and length ($L$) dominate ($>70\%$ combined attribution), verifying that the models extracted the Hiramatsu-Oka quadratic scaling ($F_f \propto d_0^2$).

4. INTERACTIVE VIRTUAL TESTING PLATFORM & CASE STUDY

4.1 System Architecture

The computational models are deployed in an interactive Streamlit web application (app.py), organized into four tabs: 1. Tab 1: Single-Particle Virtual UTM & Sieve Lab 2. Tab 2: Multi-Scale Size & Shape Scaling Simulator (Inverse Design) 3. Tab 3: Auxiliary Computer Vision Aggregate Scanner 4. Tab 4: Model Benchmarks & Validation Dashboard

4.2 Tab 1: Virtual UTM & Post-Breakage Sieve Lab

Tab 1 acts as a digital Universal Testing Machine: - Users select material (RC, RB, RM) and adjust continuous sliders for dimensions ($L, I, S$). - Outputs instant cards for $\sigma_f, F_f, E_f, D$, breakage mode, and Weibull survival probability. - Displays a simulated force-displacement curve with non-linear Hertzian pre-peak stiffening up to peak rupture load, alongside the complete post-crushing sieve curve (Figure 4.1).

Figure 4.1: Program Screenshot - Tab 1 Virtual UTM and Sieve Analysis

Figure 4.1: Program screenshot from Tab 1. Left: Predicted post-crushing sieve gradation curve. Right: Simulated force-displacement response with annotated peak failure load.

4.3 Tab 2: Multi-Scale Scaling Simulator (Inverse Design)

Tab 2 features the Inverse Design Transformer (src/inverse_designer.py). It accepts a baseline particle and projects how crushing strength evolves across sizes ($5\text{–}35\text{ mm}$) and sphericities ($\Phi = 0.4\text{–}0.9$): - 2D Scaling Heatmap: Displays continuous strength with a star marker overlaying the user's particle (Figure 4.2). - Physical Scaling Subplots: Plots size-scaling curves overlaid with experimental laboratory data points from Liang et al. (2025) and Cai et al. (2024) (Figure 4.3).

Figure 4.2: Program Screenshot - Tab 2 2D Scaling Heatmap

Figure 4.3: Program Screenshot - Tab 2 Experimental Validation Subplots

Figure 4.3: Program screenshot from Tab 2. Model size-scaling curves overlaid with published experimental benchmark points from Liang et al. (2025) and Cai et al. (2024).

4.4 Tab 3: Auxiliary Computer Vision Scanner

Tab 3 provides an exploratory image processing utility: - Applies adaptive Otsu thresholding and contour extraction to top-down photographs. - Fits minimum-area bounding boxes to determine major ($L$) and intermediate ($I$) axes. - Approximates out-of-plane thickness using stereological aspect ratios ($S \approx 0.65 I$). - Automatically sends measured dimensions to the ML prediction pipeline.

Scope Note: Tab 3 serves as an auxiliary dimensioning utility. The core scientific contribution of this B.Tech project is the physics-informed mechanical modeling and experimental validation.

5.3 Conclusions

This B.Tech Project successfully developed, benchmarked, and validated a Physics-Informed Machine Learning platform for recycled aggregate crushing mechanics: 1. Coupled Dataset: Successfully coupled size-dependent Weibull fracture with 3D sphericity power laws ($N = 3,600$). 2. High Accuracy: CatBoost achieved Mean $R^2 = 0.962$, with peak force achieving $R^2 = 0.987$. 3. Mechanistic Validity: SHAP confirmed that models honor Hiramatsu-Oka quadratic scaling ($F_f \propto d_0^2$) and Cai shape power laws. 4. Experimental Agreement: Continuous model predictions matched published laboratory data with an MAE of $0.043\text{ MPa}$ ($1.15\%$ MAPE). 5. Practical Tool: The Streamlit web suite enables rapid, non-destructive virtual testing for quarry screening, crusher energy optimization, and pavement subgrade design.

5.4 Future Work

  1. DEM Bulk Coupling: Integrate single-particle predictions into bulk Discrete Element Method simulations to model multi-particle pavement compaction.
  2. 3D Depth Imaging: Upgrade the computer vision pipeline with structured-light depth cameras to measure the out-of-plane shortest axis ($S$) directly.
